boards.name: Arduino Uno R3
boards.pwmSummary: 6 PWM pins (~490/980 Hz), no hardware DAC
boards.bestFor: Absolute beginners, 5V sensors, breadboard & shield learning
boards.overview: The classic 5V teaching board. Simple, predictable, and forgiving for beginners learning digital I/O, analogRead(), PWM, and basic robotics without complex voltage shifting.
boards.voltageWarning: I/O pins operate at 5V (max ~20 mA recommended per pin, 40 mA absolute max). Do not connect 3.3V-only sensor logic lines directly without a level shifter.
pinHighlights: 14 digital I/O pins (D0/D1 are shared with USB Serial — avoid using D0/D1 for LEDs/buttons while debugging).
6 hardware PWM pins marked with ~ (D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11).
6 analog inputs A0–A5 with 10-bit resolution (0 to 1023 representing 0V to 5V).
External interrupts on D2 and D3; I2C on A4 (SDA) / A5 (SCL); SPI on D10–D13.
ideSetupSteps: Install Arduino IDE 2.x from arduino.cc.
Open Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager and confirm 'Arduino AVR Boards' is installed.
Connect the Uno R3 via USB-B cable.
Select Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno.
Select the detected COM / tty port under Tools -> Port.
boards.codeNote: On Uno R3, analogRead() returns 0–1023 (10-bit) and analogWrite() accepts 0–255 on PWM pins (~).

boards.name: Arduino Uno R4
boards.digitalPins: 14 (6 PWM, plus true 12-bit DAC on A0)
boards.bestFor: Higher-speed 5V robotics, CAN bus, Wi-Fi/LED Matrix (R4 WiFi)
boards.overview: Keeps the familiar 5V Uno form factor while upgrading to a 32-bit 48 MHz ARM processor, 256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM, hardware CAN bus, and a true 12-bit DAC.
boards.voltageWarning: Still 5V logic on GPIO pins, but per-pin current sourcing/sinking is lower (~8 mA recommended on RA4M1) than the older ATmega328P! Always use resistors and transistors/drivers for loads.
pinHighlights: Available in two official editions: Uno R4 Minima (USB-C, SWD) and Uno R4 WiFi (adds ESP32-S3 co-processor + 12x8 LED Matrix + Qwiic I2C).
Supports 10-bit default ADC or higher resolution via analogReadResolution(14).
Pin A0 doubles as a true 12-bit Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC).
AVR-specific register code (like TCCR1A or PORTB) will NOT compile on Uno R4.
ideSetupSteps: Open Arduino IDE -> Boards Manager.
Search for and install 'Arduino UNO R4 Boards'.
Connect the board using a USB-C data cable.
Select either 'Arduino UNO R4 Minima' or 'Arduino UNO R4 WiFi' under Tools -> Board.
Choose the active serial port and verify with Blink.

variants.name: Uno R4 Minima
variants.notes: No Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and no LED Matrix; includes SWD debug connector.

variants.name: Uno R4 WiFi
variants.notes: Adds Wi-Fi/BLE, built-in 12x8 red LED matrix, and 3.3V Qwiic I2C port.

boards.codeNote: Uno R4 supports analogReadResolution(12) or (14) for finer sensor precision than Uno R3.

boards.name: Arduino Nano Family
boards.bestFor: Compact breadboard prototypes, wearable & small mobile robots
boards.overview: The Arduino Nano name covers a breadboard-friendly form factor spanning very different microcontrollers. Never assume two Nano boards share the same voltage, core, or bootloader.
boards.voltageWarning: CRITICAL: Nano Classic and Nano Every use 5V logic, whereas Nano 33 IoT, Nano 33 BLE, and Nano ESP32 use STRICT 3.3V logic. Applying 5V to a 3.3V Nano pin can permanently destroy the chip.
pinHighlights: Nano Classic (ATmega328P) has A6 and A7 as analog-input-only pins — they cannot be used with digitalWrite().
Many clone Nano Classic boards use a CH340 USB-to-Serial chip and the 'ATmega328P (Old Bootloader)' option.
Nano Every (ATmega4809) offers 48 KB Flash and 6 KB SRAM at 5V with a separate hardware Serial1 on D0/D1.
Nano ESP32 uses 3.3V logic, USB-C, and Arduino pin numbering vs GPIO numbering options.
ideSetupSteps: Identify your exact Nano board label before plugging in sensors.
For Nano Classic: install 'Arduino AVR Boards' -> select Arduino Nano -> check Processor (ATmega328P vs Old Bootloader).
For Nano Every: install 'Arduino megaAVR Boards' -> select Arduino Nano Every.
For Nano ESP32: install 'Arduino ESP32 Boards' -> select Arduino Nano ESP32.

variants.name: Arduino Nano (Classic)
variants.notes: Mini-USB; A6/A7 analog-only; watch for Old Bootloader option on older/clone boards.

variants.name: Arduino Nano Every
variants.notes: Micro-USB; 3x SRAM of Classic (6 KB); Serial1 on D0/D1 is independent of USB Serial.

variants.name: Arduino Nano ESP32
variants.notes: USB-C; Wi-Fi + BLE; NEVER feed 5V into GPIO pins.

boards.codeNote: Remember that on Nano Classic, pins A6 and A7 only work with analogRead(), never digitalWrite().

boards.name: Arduino Mega 2560
boards.bestFor: Multi-sensor robots, 3D printers, robotic arms, multi-UART systems
boards.overview: Built for large-scale 5V robotics projects that outgrow the Uno's pin count and memory. Offers 256 KB Flash, 8 KB SRAM, 54 digital pins, 16 analog inputs, and 4 hardware serial ports.
boards.voltageWarning: 5V logic like the Uno R3, but do not draw high total current across all 54 pins simultaneously (respect total port and Vcc/GND current limits; power motors and servos from an external supply with shared GND).
pinHighlights: 4 independent hardware UARTs: Serial (USB), Serial1 (18/19), Serial2 (16/17), Serial3 (14/15) — eliminates fragile SoftwareSerial.
15 PWM pins (D2–D13 and D44–D46) for controlling multiple servos and motor drivers.
SPI pins differ from Uno R3: MISO=50, MOSI=51, SCK=52, SS=53.
I2C pins are D20 (SDA) and D21 (SCL).
ideSetupSteps: Ensure 'Arduino AVR Boards' is installed in Boards Manager.
Connect the Mega 2560 via USB-B cable.
Select Tools -> Board -> Arduino Mega or Mega 2560.
Confirm Tools -> Processor -> ATmega2560 (Mega 2560).
Select the serial port and upload.
boards.codeNote: Mega 2560 lets you talk to GPS/Bluetooth modules on Serial1 while keeping USB Serial free for debugging.

boards.name: ESP32 Family
boards.analogInputs: 12-bit ADC (0–4095; ADC2 conflicts with Wi-Fi on classic ESP32)
boards.pwmSummary: LEDC hardware PWM on most output-capable GPIOs
boards.bestFor: Connected robotics, Wi-Fi/BLE telemetry, fast multi-tasking control
boards.overview: A high-performance 3.3V microcontroller family with integrated Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Different ESP32 silicon variants have distinct CPU cores, pinouts, USB peripherals, and ADC rules.
boards.voltageWarning: STRICT 3.3V LOGIC ONLY. Never connect 5V sensor outputs (such as an HC-SR04 Echo pin powered at 5V) directly to an ESP32 GPIO without a voltage divider or logic level shifter.
pinHighlights: On classic ESP32-WROOM-32, GPIO 34, 35, 36, and 39 are INPUT-ONLY and have no internal pull-up resistors.
Avoid pulling boot strapping pins (e.g., GPIO 0, 2, 12, 15 on classic ESP32) to the wrong state at reset.
12-bit ADC returns 0–4095 instead of Arduino Uno's 0–1023.
Use analogWrite() in Arduino-ESP32 v3.x or LEDC APIs; note that ESP32-C3 is single-core RISC-V while ESP32-S3 is dual-core Xtensa LX7 with native USB.
ideSetupSteps: Open Arduino IDE -> Preferences -> Additional Boards Manager URLs and add Espressif's official ESP32 package index URL.
Open Boards Manager, search 'esp32 by Espressif Systems', and install.
Select your exact board variant (e.g., ESP32 Dev Module, ESP32S3 Dev Module, or ESP32C3 Dev Module).
If upload stalls at 'Connecting...', hold the BOOT button briefly when prompted by the IDE.

variants.name: ESP32-WROOM-32 (Classic)
variants.notes: Wi-Fi + Classic BT + BLE; GPIO 34–39 are input-only; ADC2 cannot be used while Wi-Fi is active; external USB-UART bridge.

variants.name: ESP32-S3
variants.notes: Wi-Fi + BLE 5 (no Classic BT); native USB-OTG; extra GPIOs and vector instructions for DSP/tinyML.

variants.name: ESP32-C3
variants.notes: Low-power compact variant; Wi-Fi + BLE 5; fewer GPIOs; built-in USB Serial/JTAG controller.

boards.codeNote: ESP32 analogRead() uses 12-bit resolution (0–4095) and 3.3V reference; stick to ADC1 pins (e.g., GPIO 32–35 on WROOM-32) when using Wi-Fi.
